newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia's grain imports may shrink in 1997 - trade.
newsitem.headline: Russia's grain imports may shrink in 1997 - trade.

text.p: Russia's private commodity traders could import less grain this year as farm output stabilises and cash shortages and falling livestock numbers reduce the country's appetite, analysts and traders said on Monday.
The Agriculture Ministry said it had targeted 1997 net grain production at 70.0 million tonnes, little changed from the official total of a net 69.3 million tonnes in 1996.
It was the first official indication of what this year's harvest would be -- and a number that, if reached, would signal yet another year of poor grain output.

"Grain imports of all types were six million tonnes in the 1995/96 (July/June) crop year and this year (1996/97) they could be around four million tonnes," said Andrei Sizov, president of independent agricultural consultancy SovEcon Ltd.
A Moscow-based dealer at a major Western trading firm said: "I'm sure there will not be great demand for imports this year.
"I agree that certainly there should be no more than last year. Demand is likely to be flat."

The government was once one of the world's biggest grain buyers but withdrew completely from the market last year because of a lack of cash and credits. Top officials have said the government will not import grain in 1997.
While grain for human consumption was likely to stay level, grain experts said animal feed demand should drop after high slaughter rates in recent years reduced cattle numbers.
A Western analyst based in Moscow said he saw little sign of interest in grain imports so far this year.
"I don't see any signs that the Russians are really needing to import large amounts of grain through commercial entities," he said.
The analyst said he expected some imports later in 1997, adding that levels this year would be little changed on 1996.
State Customs Committee data showed 1996 grain and flour imports nearly doubled on 1995 to 5.1 million tonnes, providing a growing niche for trading powerhouses active in Russia.

Sizov attributed the expected decline in 1997 import needs to a shift towards higher wheat output. Last year wheat's share in overall Russian grain output rose to around 50 percent. He gave no comparison for 1995.
Sizov said that if demand for wheat turned out to be unchanged, as he expected, import needs would fall.
"Last year (1995/96) Russia imported 3.2 million tonnes of wheat but this year (wheat) imports will be around 2.0 million tonnes," he said.
"And feed grain demand is actually going to go down due to the decline in livestock numbers."
Last year's net grain harvest of 69.3 million tonnes was up on 1995's 63.4 million but was still one of the worst in the past 30 years.
Russia regularly produced more than 100 million tonnes annually in the 1970s and 1980s.
But analysts said Russia might have to get used to smaller crops in the medium term.
"I think that 70 million tonnes may now be considered the normal level under current (growing) conditions," the Western analyst said.
Traders said grain output might be higher than official figures show, with farmers keeping some grain in storage to sell privately.
Analysts have said "hidden" grain could represent as much as 10 percent of the total crop.
"Farmers don't always tell the whole story. They say that their crop is small but on the black market you see grain being traded," the trader said.
